extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of aesthetics, philosophy of art, and humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Kant's aesthetic criteria for what produces laughter, wit, naiveté, and humour — i.e., theoretical principles for evaluating or crafting humorous effects. Focuses on cognitive mechanics (expectation, deception, absurdity), presentation, and bodily effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity as prerequisite for convulsive laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: In everything that is to excite a lively convulsive laugh there must be something absurd (in which the Understanding, therefore, can find no satisfaction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic stimulus must present an absurdity such that the Understanding cannot find satisfaction in it; this lack of cognitive satisfaction is central to producing a convulsive laugh. The absurd element triggers the sudden cognitive change described elsewhere (expectation → nothing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter arises from sudden transformation of a strained expectation into nothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is an affection arising from the sudden transformation of a strained expectation into nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The joke/story should build an expectation (a 'strained' tension) and then abruptly dissipate it into nothing rather than into a substantive opposite. Examples: the Indian astonished at beer foaming out ('I wonder how you ever got it in'), the heir who can't make mourners look sad. Anti-patterns: if the expectation is simply exposed as false without comic reversal (immediate detection of falsehood) it displeases rather than amuses; if it turns into a positive opposite (something still present) it can cause grief instead of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Momentary deception (illusion) is required
rubrics_metrics.description: The jest must contain something that is capable of deceiving for a moment; when the illusion is dissipated the mind jerks back and oscillates, producing laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct jokes so they plausibly deceive the audience briefly; the enjoyment comes from the rapid alternation of tension (expectation) and relaxation (dissipation). The transient deception should be believable enough to engage the understanding, but brief enough to be dissolved for the humorous effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: sudden (not gradual) relaxation of tension
rubrics_metrics.description: The strain on the cord as it were is suddenly (and not gradually) relaxed, which must occasion the mental movement and bodily oscillation corresponding to laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective humor depends on abrupt timing — a rapid release of expectation rather than a slow unwinding. Delivery and placement of the punch (or twist) are essential; gradual deflation reduces the comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation must be transformed into nothing (not into the positive opposite)
rubrics_metrics.description: It does not transform itself into the positive opposite of an expected object—for then there would still be something, which might even be a cause of grief—but it must be transformed into nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the resolution removes the anticipated content entirely rather than replacing it with another substantive outcome. Replacing the expectation with an opposite may retain emotional weight (grief, anger) and thus fails to produce the light oscillatory pleasure of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and manner (assumed seriousness) influence comedic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The way a story is told (assumed seriousness, circumstantial description, manner of delivery) affects whether it produces laughter — telling with assumed gravity can heighten the comic reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diction, tone, and sincerity strategically: an ostentatiously serious presentation of an absurdity or naiveté often amplifies the effect. Example: the same tale of a liar vs. a simpleton told differently produces very different audience reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour as play of thought (wit) distinct from music and games
rubrics_metrics.description: The play of thought (wit) springs merely from the change of representations in the Judgement; by it no thought that brings an interest with it is produced, but yet the mind is animated thereby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour/wit operates at the level of cognitive representations — altering how the mind judges a representation — and thus should be crafted as conceptual play (incongruity, re-interpretation) rather than as material reward or sensory alteration (games/music).

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary assumption of a comic mental disposition (humour as talent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour in the good sense means the talent of being able voluntarily to put oneself into a certain mental disposition, in which everything is judged quite differently from the ordinary method (reversed, in fact), and yet in accordance with certain rational principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective humour often depends on an author's or performer's skill to adopt and sustain a 'reversed' evaluative stance deliberately and coherently. Distinguish this from involuntary moodiness ('a man of humours'); cultivated humour is purposeful and principled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naiveté as a comic device (representation of innocent simplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Naiveté is the breaking out of the sincerity originally natural to humanity in opposition to that art of dissimulation which has become a second nature; we laugh at the simplicity that does not understand how to dissemble, and yet are delighted when nature thwarts assumed manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use naiveté as a contrast to artifice: representing a character's genuine unspoiled simplicity can expose social dissimulation and provoke laughter mixed with compassion. In fiction, representing naiveté is a rare but beautiful art; do not conflate it with mere open-hearted simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bodily mechanism: alternating tension/relaxation produces gratification
rubrics_metrics.description: The sudden transposition of the mind corresponds to an alternating tension and relaxation of the elastic portions of our intestines, communicating to the diaphragm and lungs, producing bodily movement (expulsion of air) that is the proper cause of the gratification in laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that part of comic pleasure is physiological: comedic devices that produce quick mental oscillation will tend to induce the bodily responses constitutive of laughter. This links timing and cognitive structure to their somatic effects and explains why humor feels 'healthful' or animating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour belongs to pleasant (not beautiful) art and prizes originality
rubrics_metrics.description: The humorous manner is near akin to the gratification that proceeds from laughter and belongs to the originality of spirit, but not to the talent of beautiful art; it is rather a pleasant than a beautiful art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or aiming for humour, prioritize originality of perspective and amusement rather than the criteria of 'beautiful' art (intrinsic seriousness, permanent conceptual worth). Humour's value is in pleasant animation rather than lasting conceptual products.
